item.title: How to Regulate Your Emotions
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

How to Regulate Your Emotions

The regulated person is adaptive and has zhong he 中和—emotional harmony.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • People who regulate their emotions can analyze information because they can pull back and think rationally.
  • When we are emotionally agile and flexible, we can balance different needs across life domains.
  • The flexible thinker reshapes his mental resources without getting entangled in unhelpful thinking patterns.

An emotionally healthy individual can regulate his emotions and adjust them to whatever his surroundings demand. People who can modulate their facial expressions while looking at emotion-filled images have better mental health than those who cannot. Showing our emotions is part of everyday social interaction. When a friend tells us she met someone special, we should show her our interest and enthusiasm. According to Columbia University professor George Bonanno and his colleague Charles Burton, a research scientist at Yale University, we must sometimes show more or less emotion than we feel. Bonanno and Burton developed the Flexible Regulation of Emotional Expression Scale, which measures expressive flexibility. Items on the scale include:

You receive a gift from a family member, but it’s a shirt you dislike. You have to show happy enthusiasm.

You’re attending the funeral of someone you don’t know. You have to be somber.

You’re a guest at a solemn religious ceremony, and the person sitting next to you just whispered a funny joke. You have to stifle your laughter.

People who regulate their emotions can quickly analyze new information because they can pull back and think rationally. This ability helps a person see possibilities and adapt to new situations. It also helps us set aside knee-jerk reactions and solve problems that come up. People who can regulate how they feel generally have better relationships, romantic, professional, and otherwise.

Emotionally regulated people are also agile thinkers; agility can halt heated emotional reactions that bring on feelings of overwhelm and paralysis. Essentially, strong emotions restrict the brain from problem-solving; however, an agile thinker can brainstorm solutions.

Many areas of therapeutic inquiry—including Gestalt, cognitive behavioral, and acceptance and commitment therapies—promote this go-with-the-flow unflappability. Psychologist Steven Hayes, developer of acceptance and commitment therapy, has examined this ability. As the author of Get Out of Your Mind and Into Your Life, Hayes may be a bit Buddhist.

Hayes and his colleagues derived the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire, which measures just how mentally rigid a person can be, and they determined that a rigid person has the following negative tendencies:

Source: AI Assisted

  • Ruminates more and can get stuck in pessimistic loops

  • Feels more anxious

  • Feels more depressed

  • Fears failure and success

  • Seeks perfection

  • Seeks approval from others

  • Suffers more mental health conditions—including mood disorders and beyond

  • Suffers an inability to learn, be curious, or be open and relies on habitual responses

  • Cannot expand or grow with new experiences

  • Falls into self-sabotaging behaviors such as substance abuse, eating disorders, and procrastination

When we are emotionally agile and flexible, we can balance different needs across life domains; we make conscious choices about time and energy on work, home, health, and other areas. The flexible thinker reshapes his mental resources and accesses different perspectives by observing his thoughts and feelings without getting entangled in unhelpful thinking patterns. This person is light on his feet and adaptive rather than maladaptive because he realizes thoughts and feelings are not an accurate reflection of reality, which allows a more flexible view of life situations. He is resilient and doesn’t buckle in the face of adversity by engaging in self-compassion, which builds inner strength. He is broad-minded and doesn’t rely on one tool or method to get through life; he tests different strategies to see what works and what doesn’t.

If we can manage our thoughts and emotions with present-moment awareness, we may better attain what we want in life—the things we value. When we get mired in our heads about slights, annoyances, grievances, fears, criticisms, insults, or whatever gloom we glom onto, we don’t pay attention to what matters. We forget what is meaningful. Ruminating on a negative thought can take us away from engaging with the things that are vital to us, what we value.

item.title: When Your Friend Is a Therapist
item.description:
Friends

When Your Friend Is a Therapist

The benefits and challenges when your friend is also a therapist

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • As friends, therapists come with many benefits but also challenges.
  • Therapists can cultivate deep connections and may expect this of their friends.
  • Therapists sometimes behave like therapists in their professional lives.
  • The therapy approach of therapists may be reflected in their interpersonal styles.

I once met a man who learned I was a psychologist and said, “I dated a therapist. I miss our deep conversations.” My husband affirmed this observation—yes, our talks were atypical. This prompted me to consider the unique qualities of having a therapist as a friend.

When I meet new people and they learn what I do, some gravitate to me, and others run the other way. One friend collected friends who were therapists, and another was anxious that I might analyze her. What do these encounters reveal about the benefits and challenges of having a therapist for a friend?

What are therapists like in their social lives?
Source: AI-generated; ChatGPT/OpenAI, 2026.

Perhaps a professional hazard is that I crave depth from my conversations with others and often take the lead in a conversation. This could simply reflect my own inclinations and disposition. I am more of an open book than other therapists I know. I push myself to take risks in becoming vulnerable in order to create intimacy. In contrast, I know other therapists who adopt a “blank slate” role in their social exchanges and do not expose themselves so readily.

In this sense, my therapy approach is reflected not only in my work but also in how I am in my personal life. As a humanistic-existentialist—a strengths-based and meaning-oriented therapist—I’m not as neutral in my listening as some of my psychoanalytic friends. I offer encouragement, I join with my friends’ challenges, I express colorful reactions, I embrace my opinions, I admit to my judgments (see former post on judgments), and I look for meaning. In fact, I’m quite relieved to be able to fully reveal myself in my friendships and have a space that can also be about me when my work is so focused on others.

My therapy approach is reflected in my parenting style as well. Before children, I imagined myself acting like a behaviorist and effectively shaping their every action. Instead, my humanistic roots came out as I harnessed their strengths to work flexibly with their problems.

I gravitate to therapists in my own social life. I find our shared values in connection and conversation to be especially fulfilling. We see the value of socializing and nurturing closeness. We know from the research and our professional experience that positive relationships reduce depression, enhance quality of life, and promote general health (WHO, 2025).

I notice how the professional background of my therapist friends colors our interactions. My social worker buddies send me links to relevant resources at the end of our conversations. My psychoanalytic pals tend to maintain a neutral, listening position in our chats. My cognitive behavioral contacts encourage me to test the reality of my fears. My humanistic-existential comrades validate and share in my feelings with me. All make valuable contributions to my life, not unlike working with different kinds of therapists as a client.

It can be difficult not to act like therapists in our personal lives. In one case, I was amused when a therapist friend abruptly ended our lunch at the 50-minute mark. Recently, a therapist friend teased me about my tendency to apply diagnoses in casual conversation. We have been conditioned to behave a certain way with others, which can lead to social habits that are hard to shake.

Little has been written on therapist friendships. Most writing related to this topic cautions the public that your therapist is not your friend. To my knowledge, Dr. Maria Baratta (2023) has one of the few pieces on therapists as friends in a previous Psychology Today blog post. She noted the empathy, confidentiality, and listening skills that can characterize us as companions.

In a rare article on this issue, Dr. Marilyn Schwartz (2021) wrote about the essential nature of friendship for the ethical practice of therapists. We rely on consultation with close colleagues to offer insights into the challenges that arise in our work. We recognize that a vibrant social life is critical to the self-care of practitioners and can help prevent burnout.

In sum, core themes emerge about the benefits and challenges of therapist friends:

  • Therapist friends may have deep conversations but struggle with small talk.
  • Therapist friends are often reliable, but might expect predictability and regularity in return.
  • Therapist friends may be emotionally available, but with boundaries that can be firm.
  • Therapist friends have insights into others, but may have trouble turning off their observations.
  • Therapist friends have done a lot of self-work, but might surprise you with their imperfections.

What are your thoughts about therapists as friends? Feel free to weigh in. I’m listening!

item.title: Dolly Parton vs. the Cult of Authenticity
item.description:
Authenticity

Dolly Parton vs. the Cult of Authenticity

Genuine authenticity is not the same as exposure.

Posted August 28, 2026

Dolly Parton at the Lanxess Arena in Cologne on July 5, 2014
Source: Josef Just/Wikimedia Commons

Few public figures appeared more unmistakably themselves than Dolly Parton. Her wigs, makeup, voice, humor, stories, and rhinestone-studded image became so familiar that they eventually seemed inseparable from the woman herself. Yet there was something paradoxical about Dolly. She built one of the most recognizable personas in modern culture while retaining an unusual degree of control over what the public could know about her, and a legitimately private life beyond.

A modern perversion of authenticity conflates it with transparency. Support for this misguided understanding amounts to what some have called a "cult of authenticity," which encourages embracing maximum vulnerability and removing masks that prevent others from seeing us as we really are. Privacy often appears suspect within this framework. Boundaries can look defensive.

The public Dolly was not merely a disguise concealing the real Dolly. Still, by her own account, the public Dolly was indeed one of her creations: an artistic, commercial, and psychological achievement assembled over decades. The hair, humor, storytelling, glamour, and stagecraft were part of her, yes. But she herself said that all of that was a relatively small part of her. And what of the larger part of her? Beyond carefully curated anecdotes, repeated time and again, we may know far less than you think.

Erving Goffman observed decades ago that human beings are always presenting themselves. We occupy roles, adapt to circumstances, and move among different social worlds. The self we bring to a funeral differs from the self we bring to a dinner party. The self we bring to a workplace differs from the self we bring to a marriage. Most people understand this.

There is an important difference between deception, performance, and privacy. Deception presents something false in order to manipulate others. Performance highlights and develops certain aspects of the self for a particular audience or purpose. Privacy preserves those aspects of the self that do not belong to the audience.

The cult of authenticity tends to collapse these categories. If a person withholds information, they risk being viewed as guarded. If they present different aspects of themselves in different settings, they may be accused of inconsistency. The ideal increasingly becomes a kind of perpetual and progressive self-disclosure.

No audience is entitled to the whole self. No employer or online following possesses an unlimited claim on another person's interior life. A healthy boundary is not a lie. Privacy is not pathology. Selective self-disclosure is not necessarily avoidance.

Dolly Parton reads to children in the Library of Congress Great Hall in 2018
Source: Shawn Miller/Wikimedia Commons

Parton's public life offers a useful illustration. Few entertainers appeared warmer or more accessible. Audiences felt connected to her. They laughed with her, grieved with her, and followed her across generations. Yet there remained parts of her life that belonged only to her. She shared generously while retaining authority over what remained her own. Far from diminishing connection, those boundaries may have made connection sustainable.

Her Imagination Library has distributed over 332 million books to children without asking anything in return. No one needed to know anything about Dolly to participate. Her public persona was large enough to attract attention but not so self-absorbed that attention became its ultimate purpose.

Hannah Arendt drew a distinction between what a person is and who a person is. The former can be catalogued and described. The latter emerges indirectly through action. Throughout her career, Dolly resisted the expectation that visibility should grant unlimited access to the person behind it. She allowed herself to be known through what she created, what she gave, and what she did rather than through endless revelation.

Human flourishing does not require complete exposure. A psychologically healthy person is not necessarily one who dismantles every boundary, confesses every private thought, or transforms every corner of life into public property. Some forms of integrity depend upon preserving a space that remains beyond the reach of audiences and institutions. There are things about a person that can be shared, and there are things that should remain under that person's stewardship alone.

Dolly Parton, 1977
Source: RCA Records/Wikimedia Commons

Dolly Parton's achievement was not that she gave the world everything. It was that she gave the world a great deal while maintaining boundaries and retaining relative ownership and control of her private life.

The cult of authenticity tells us that the path to psychological health lies through ever-greater transparency. Parton's life suggests a different possibility. A person can be theatrical, curated, personally boundaried, and deeply real all at the same time.

One of the most authentic things a person can do is decide what parts of themselves belong to the world and what parts do not.

item.title: The Process of Choosing a Surrogate
item.description:
Infertility

The Process of Choosing a Surrogate

The emotional steps that come before choosing the right surrogate.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • The relationship with a surrogate begins before pregnancy; preparing for the journey you will share.
  • Choosing a surrogate begins with understanding your own emotional readiness and expectations.
  • Compatibility is less about similarity and more about trust, communication, and shared expectations.
Source: Olena Yakobchuk / Shutterstock

I've come to think of choosing a surrogate as a series of stages, with each one building upon the last, gradually moving you from loss toward hope, and from searching for the "perfect match" to building the right relationship.

Often there is an outward focus on finding the "right" woman, but with that focus, some important preparatory steps can be missed. In reality, the journey begins by looking inward.

Am I ready?

Before all the logistical steps and assessments, it's worth considering your own level of readiness. Not that anyone can be completely ready for something they have never done before, but certain questions are useful to consider:

Have I taken time to grieve what brought me here?

Have I begun to shift from surviving infertility to preparing for parenthood?

Am I emotionally ready to enter a relationship that requires trust, vulnerability, and shared uncertainty?

A lot of patience and discipline is required to not rush through these questions while you're dealing with a lot of tiredness — the tiredness of repeated medical interventions, the waiting, the hoping, and the loss. The thought of finally moving forward towards a different ending can offer much-needed relief.

But its worth slowing down, as this person will carry your baby and has the potential to form one of the most unique and meaningful relationships of your lives.

Stage One: Making Space for Grief

Almost nobody arrives at surrogacy because it was their first choice.

Surrogacy is usually reached after multiple rounds of failed IVF, miscarriages, recurrent implantation failure, and sometimes years of hoping that the next treatment would be the "one."

Yet, before all these feelings can be resolved, many intended parents move to choose a surrogate before they've had time to fully acknowledge what they're leaving behind: their ideas and story of the pregnancy and birth they imagined.

While this step isn't about "getting over it," it can be important to rest, even for a few weeks, to feel what you need to feel and to acknowledge the tremendous flexibility it has taken to choose a new path.

Making space for this is important because grief that isn't acknowledged has an uncanny way of showing up later. Some of the same feelings you’ve experienced before can begin to surface as anxiety, a need for control, unrealistic expectations, or difficulty trusting the process.

After all, it can be difficult to hand over something as important as a pregnancy to someone else. A delayed response to a text may create far more anxiety than expected. A surrogate making a choice differently from how you would make it yourself may feel unexpectedly threatening. Or the excitement of finally being matched may come with sadness, or even resentment, as this is not how you imagined becoming a parent.

These reactions do not necessarily mean that something is wrong. Sometimes they are simply signs that experiences from the journey that came before are precipitating into the one that is beginning.

The goal before matching with a surrogate is to recognize that grief and hope can exist together.

Stage Two: Moving From Urgency to Intention

"I just want this to work. I mean, we’ve waited SOOO long, been through multiple rounds of sh@t. I need to be done with this." — Tracy

You probably recognize this feeling. When people have experienced repeated disappointment, it's understandable to feel a sense of urgency.

It’s not about getting rid of that feeling but rather making sure your actions aren’t being driven by overwhelm. Urgency can quietly become the loudest voice in the room.

In reality, this can manifest as a question: "Can we make this work?" rather than "Is this the right match?" Those are very different questions.

The best decisions come when there is enough emotional space to be curious and honest rather than simply relieved.

Stage Three: Looking Beyond the Checklist

Of course, medical screening matters, previous pregnancy matters, and clinic approval matters. But those things don't build a relationship.

Surrogacy is one of the few experiences where two families walk together through enormous uncertainty.

The real questions become:

Can we communicate when things don't go according to plan?

Can we repair our misunderstandings?

Can we tolerate uncertainty together?

In short, psychological flexibility often matters far more than similarity. You don't need someone who shares your hobbies, but someone who shares your willingness to navigate the unexpected with honesty and respect.

Stage Four: Listening to Your Nervous System

After meeting a surrogate, I often ask intended parents a question they don't expect:

"How did you feel when you left the meeting?"

Not what you thought, but what you felt.

Did you feel calmer? Did you feel heard?

We can sometimes register a sense of emotional safety or unease before we can easily put into words why. And while that feeling shouldn't make the entire decision for you, it does deserve your attention. Understanding what feels comfortable or familiar to us, and why, can give us useful information when making this decision.

Stage Five: Knowing When to Stop Searching

Surrogacy matching can create the illusion that if you ask enough questions, read enough profiles, and meet enough potential surrogates, eventually you will feel clear and pick the right one.

This makes sense given the context. After infertility, uncertainty feels traumatic. So much has already gone wrong that it makes sense to want reassurance that this time you are making exactly the right decision. As a result, it can become tempting to keep looking for the person who removes every doubt.

But there is no perfect surrogate, just as there is no completely predictable pregnancy or surrogacy journey.

At some point, choosing requires a different psychological task: moving from evaluating to trusting. That doesn't mean talking yourself into a match that doesn't feel right. It means recognizing the difference between a genuine concern and the understandable wish for absolute certainty after years of uncertainty.

Something to ask yourself:

Is there something about this person that genuinely concerns me, or am I frightened because choosing her means I finally have something to lose again?

Sometimes readiness isn't the absence of doubt.

The Journey Before the Journey

People often ask me what makes a good surrogate match. While there isn't a standard answer, I usually respond with a question:

"Who are you now, before you begin looking?"

I ask this question because choosing a surrogate isn't only about finding the right person, it’s about understanding what you are also bringing into the relationship—your grief, hopes, biases, fears and fantasies, and your understandable wish for things finally to go right.

The goal isn't to arrive at matching perfectly—that's unrealistic—but rather to know your feelings well enough that they don't drive the bus for you.

And that work begins long before the first profile is ever opened.

item.title: Why AuDHD Can Be More Challenging Than Autism or ADHD Alone
item.description:
Autism

Why AuDHD Can Be More Challenging Than Autism or ADHD Alone

AuDHD, the comorbidity of autism and ADHD, is more than the sum of its parts.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Challenges with executive functions and attention are core features of autism and ADHD.
  • About 40 percent of people with autism have ADHD.
  • Until 13 years ago, a person with autism could not be given a diagnosis of ADHD.
  • Adolescents with AuDHD have more challenges with executive functions and regulation than autistic adolescents.

AuDHD is a grassroots term that arose from the neurodivergent community—largely through usage in social media—as a means to identify, learn about, and advocate for people who have both autism and ADHD.

There are surprisingly little data on the co-occurrence of autism and ADHD because these two conditions were not allowed to be diagnosed in the same individual until the publication of the DSM-5 in 2013. Prior to DSM-5, if an individual was diagnosed with autism, it was not possible for them to also be diagnosed with ADHD.

About 5 to 8 percent of children have ADHD and 2 to 4 percent have autism, according to recent literature reviewed by Canals et al. (2024). If autism and ADHD were independent of one another, it's estimated that about 0.2 percent of children would have both conditions. But autism and ADHD occur together much more than one would expect based on chance.

In a review of 63 studies, about 40 percent of autistic people had an ADHD diagnosis (Rong et al., 2021). In a more recent study from Spain, 46 percent of school-aged children with autism had ADHD and about 10 percent of children with ADHD had autism (Canals et a., 2024). Even children with sub-threshold autistic traits had a high rate of ADHD diagnoses.

Thus, it appears that the two conditions—which until recently were not formally diagnosed in the same individual—co-occur frequently. I suspect this rate might be an underestimate due to the fact that challenges with executive functions and attention are core features of both conditions.

When an individual has autism and ADHD, the challenges of living in a culture that is not equipped to embrace neurodiversity can be magnified. Social interactions can be more challenging, daily living skills can be harder to master, emotions can be more difficult to regulate, and well-being can suffer (as reviewed in Canals et al., 2024).

In one study, adolescents with AuDHD had more challenges than autistic adolescents without ADHD on measures of executive functions, taking the perspective of another person, and emotional and behavioral regulation (Rosello et al., 2023). AuDHD also had more learning difficulties. The authors asserted that executive functions, impulsivity, and challenges with regulation are important to assess in autistic children and may be why AuDHD adolescents had relatively more difficulties than autistic adolescents.

In 2024, Emma Craddock wrote a commentary to elevate the voices of girls and women with AuDHD. She visualized the synergy that having autism and ADHD presents. “We might imagine autism as the colour red, ADHD as the colour blue, and AuDHD as purple—more than a sum of its parts; a thing in and of itself,” (Craddock, 2024, p. 2163).

Autism and ADHD are more than the sum of their parts. Efforts to raise awareness and advocate for more understanding for AuDHD are vital to maximizing well-being. Early identification of ADHD in autistic children and especially the assessment of executive functions can help identify the appropriate supports and ensure the best developmental outcomes.

item.title: Why It’s Helpful to Throw Your Food Rules in The Trash
item.description:
Diet

Why It’s Helpful to Throw Your Food Rules in The Trash

How food rules create rigidity and increase distress and self-criticism.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Food rules are guidelines you have about what, when, or how much you eat, and are typically unhelpful.
  • They can create anxiety, social isolation, self-criticism, and guilt when broken, especially if held rigidly.
  • You may think of yourself as “bad” or “good” based on what you eat, and whether you follow your food rule.
  • It is helpful to make flexible food choices that honor your body and create ease and self-compassion.
Source: Fotos/unsplash

Food rules are any guidelines you have about what, when, or how much you eat. At first glance, food rules can seem helpful. For example, a person may have a guideline around needing to eat a certain amount of protein or vegetables each day, not eating a lot of sugar, or limiting carbohydrates. In some circumstances, such as having a health condition or food allergy, certain food rules may be medically necessary.

In general, however, food rules tend to do more harm than good, particularly when rigidly held and followed. This is why.

The Dark Side of Food Rules

Food rules can lead to food restriction and not eating certain foods that you define as unhealthy or “bad.” In turn, these rules can lead to anxiety, social isolation, self-criticism, and guilt, especially if held rigidly or if broken.

You may call yourself “bad” or “good” based on what you eat, and whether you strictly follow your food rule. In this way, food rules become bigger than just food. You may come to tie what you eat to who you are as a person and your sense of self. You are “good” if you ate a salad at lunch, and “bad” if you ate a donut.

Much of the time, people adopt food rules due to a fear of gaining weight or wanting to lose weight. This creates and reinforces a mindset that you are valuable and worthy only if you are a certain size and shape, which leads to feeling unworthy if you are not that size.

Further, food rules tend to be rigid. They tend to be based on an all-or-nothing mentality that does not allow for flexibility or eating in a way that respects your body. For example, you may ignore your hunger cues and stop eating even if you are still hungry because you have a rule of only eating a certain amount of food.

Restricting food or not eating certain foods can also create and maintain a restrict-binge eating cycle, such that eating high-calorie or satisfying foods is avoided, which leads to strong urges to eat these “bad” or “forbidden” foods, and feeling a loss of control and a sense that you can’t stop eating when you finally eat them. You then work hard to again avoid these foods, and the pattern becomes cyclical.

Further, rigid food rules tend to lead to a preoccupation with food. It may seem like food rules would lessen thoughts of food as they provide a structure to follow. Yet research has demonstrated that the more certain foods are regarded as forbidden, and the more people try to restrict those foods, the more preoccupied with the foods they become. In this way, food rules create more stress about food.

How to Start Letting Go of Your Food Rules

Instead of eating based on rigid rules that set you up to feel stressed, anxious, and dissatisfied, it is helpful to shift to making flexible food choices that honor your body and how you feel in the moment and create more ease and self-compassion over time.

Below are ways you can practice breaking food rules.

  • Nonjudgmentally write down your food rules. Write down all the food rules you have. Practice not judging or evaluating them. Just write them down. Add to the list as additional food rules come to mind.
  • Rank these rules as the least stressful to break to the most anxiety-inducing to break.
  • Pick one of the least stressful rules on your list and think about how you can gently change or break the rule in a safe, low-pressure environment. For example, if you have a rule of no eating after 7pm, but you notice you feel hungry around 9pm, you may practice having a snack. Then, repeatedly break the rule until it feels easy to do, and you feel emotionally neutral about it. In other words, you don’t feel guilty. Then, move on to another rule.
  • Notice any guilt you may feel after changing/breaking a food rule, and remind yourself that food is not “good” or “bad”; it just is, and your character or value as a person is not based on what you eat.
  • Focus on addition, not subtraction. Instead of thinking about restricting or not eating certain foods, adopt an addition mindset where you focus on foods you can add that allow you to feel satisfied.
  • Practice self-compassion. If you notice being self-critical or judging yourself, pause, take a breath, and repeat a self-compassionate statement to yourself, such as “This is difficult, and I am taking steps to be kind to myself.” Be patient with yourself. Changing how you think about food and eating, and breaking food rules, is not easy.

With practice, it is possible to break unhelpful food rules, feel more comfortable with your body and yourself, and feel more ease and satisfaction around food.

item.title: You Can Apologize Without Owing Your Adult Child Forever
item.description:
Parenting

You Can Apologize Without Owing Your Adult Child Forever

Owning your mistakes doesn’t mean accepting lifelong blame or responsibility.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • An apology can acknowledge pain without making the parent responsible for fixing the rest of the child’s life.
  • Parental guilt can drive repeated rescuing, financial support, or tolerance of unhealthy behavior.
  • Healthy repair allows parents to own the past while still setting calm, firm boundaries in the present.

Most parents, if they keep it real and are truthful with themselves, can easily think of things they wish they had done differently when raising their now-adult children. One Dad (Tim) of a 28-year-old struggling adult son (Ben; both are fictitious names) said some poignant things recently in a parent coaching session. He said, "Man, I think I'm guilty of all the things I should not have done with Ben. I mean, I yelled too much, I was way too critical during his soccer games, and it sucks to hear myself say, but I was often too critical when my anxiety over his future got the best of me."

Tim went on, "Dr. Jeff, it's like, what the hell was I thinking back then, because I can see it all plain as day now." As parents, I think we've all walked some days in Tim's shoes; I certainly have, at times, with my own now-adult children. Let's now look at how to handle adult children who have negative memories and continuing pain, and who struggle to let go of them.

Defensiveness Will Not Stop the Blame Bombing

When an adult child links their struggles and setbacks to their parents' mistakes, missteps, misguided advice, and all the other problematic "misses," it can feel very overwhelming for even the most nondefensive parents. Complicating matters is that the tone in which emotionally reactive adult children often bring up their past hurts can range from pressured to straight-up explosive.

A quick news bulletin for parents: If reflexively responding with "I did the best I could" worked well, I'm guessing you wouldn't be reading this article right now. Yes, I get it. You are human, and therefore imperfect like all of us human beings, and you made some unpleasant mistakes with your kids even though you likely also did many things very well for them. Still, please stop relying on "I did the best I could." "Why?" you ask, thinking you did do the best you could. Because it makes you sound tone deaf, defensive, and insensitive to the pain your adult child continues to focus on.

What Is a Better Response?

Based on my over thirty years of coaching parents of struggling adult children, I have seen that there is a far better way for you to handle your adult child blaming you for their hurts and struggles. And that is leading with accountability (without turning yourself into a human punching bag, either). For example, you can say, "I wish I handled those things differently, and I'm sorry." Just keep in mind that accountability isn't the same as handing your adult child a blank check, financially or emotionally, for the rest of your life.

An Apology Is Not a Lifelong Contract

As I explain in my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me: How to Stop Rescuing, reduce conflict, and help your adult child move forward, parents can get so caught up in trying to prove they care that they unintentionally help their adult child avoid the responsibilities that could help them grow. So, to build on the better response above, you could also say, "I know there are things from your childhood I did that hurt you. I am willing to calmly discuss them. And I am willing to listen when you're struggling. But listening and caring don't mean I'm blamed endlessly for those struggles or that I should keep solving problems for you. I believe you owe it to yourself to take the lead in working through them."

The Takeaway

You can deliver both your apology and your listening in a loving way. But just remember that taking responsibility for what belongs to you does not mean accepting responsibility for everything. In short, you can be accountable for your past without owing your adult child your future.

item.title: What Church Bells Taught Me About Our Relationship With Time
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

What Church Bells Taught Me About Our Relationship With Time

Personal Perspective: What if your sense of time isn’t really yours?

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Culture shapes how we experience time.
  • Our environment reinforces our time habits.
  • Repeated time cues can make the clock hard to ignore.

This summer, I traveled across Europe, including visits to Vienna and Salzburg. Both are beautiful cities, but as a psychologist who studies time, I found myself becoming fascinated by something much more mundane: the church bells.

Regardless of where I seemed to be in either city, I could hear time passing.

On the hour, the bells would ring. Fifteen minutes later, one ring. At the half hour, two. At 45 minutes past the hour, three. And then, before you knew it, the bells were ringing again to announce the arrival of another hour.

Time was everywhere.

Now, I should admit that I am what I call a classic “clock person.” I have written before about our relationship with clocks and how constantly monitoring time may interfere with our happiness. But even I started to become a little edgy from the continuous reminders.

Another 15 minutes gone.

Another half hour.

Another hour.

It made me wonder: What happens when you grow up surrounded by these signals?

Clock Time Versus Event Time

Psychologists and anthropologists have long observed differences in how cultures relate to time.

Some cultures tend to be more clock-oriented. Activities are organized around specific times, schedules, deadlines, and expectations of punctuality. Germany, Switzerland, and Austria are often associated with this orientation.

Other cultures are relatively more event-oriented. In countries such as Italy, Spain, and France, there may be greater flexibility around when something begins or ends. The activity itself, and the people involved in it, can play a larger role in determining when it is time to move on.

Of course, these are broad cultural tendencies, not descriptions of every individual. There are chronically late Austrians and extraordinarily punctual Italians. But cultural differences in our relationship with time are nevertheless noticeable.

And while traveling through Austria, I began thinking about those differences in a new way.

In Vienna, the trains seemed to leave precisely when they were supposed to. Concert halls closed their doors when performances began. Appointments and reservations operated according to the clock.

Everything seemed to communicate the same message:

Time matters. Pay attention to it.

And then there were those bells.

Every 15 minutes.

Does Culture Shape the Clock, or Does the Clock Shape Culture?

We usually think about cultural attitudes as something transmitted from one generation to another through parents, schools, workplaces, and social norms.

Children learn that being late is unacceptable because adults tell them so. Employees learn that deadlines matter because organizations reward or punish them accordingly. Eventually, these behaviors become norms: This is simply how we do things here.

But perhaps we underestimate the role of the physical environment in reinforcing those norms.

Imagine growing up in a place where, throughout your day, the environment itself announces the passage of time.

You don't need to look at your watch.

You don't need to check your phone.

The city tells you.

Fifteen minutes have passed.

Now 30.

Now 45.

Another hour is gone.

Day after day, year after year, generation after generation.

Could something as simple as church bells help reinforce a culture's awareness of time?

I am not suggesting that Austrian punctuality exists because churches ring their bells. Cultural attitudes toward time have complicated historical, economic, religious, and social origins.

But psychology tells us that our environments matter. Repeated cues can direct our attention and, over time, help shape habits and expectations. What surrounds us becomes part of what we perceive as normal.

And that is what struck me in Austria.

The bells weren't merely reporting the time. They were continually making time salient.

When the Environment Becomes Invisible

Perhaps the most interesting part is that people who grow up with these environmental cues may barely notice them.

I noticed the bells because I was a visitor.

Someone who has lived in Vienna for 40 years might hear them without consciously registering them at all. Yet something does not necessarily need our conscious attention to become part of the environment that shapes our behavior.

We experience this in countless other ways.

Cities teach us how quickly to walk. Transportation systems teach us how carefully to plan. Store hours influence when we shop. Meal traditions tell us when eating is appropriate. Schools teach children when to work, when to rest, and when to move to the next activity.

Eventually, these external structures become internal expectations.

The environment doesn't merely accommodate culture. It may also help reproduce it.

And Then There Are the Swiss

This becomes even more apparent when we look across the border.

Switzerland is famous for watches, precision, and timekeeping. Germany has Pünktlichkeit, punctuality, as a deeply recognizable cultural value. Austria similarly has a reputation for adherence to schedules.

Is it a coincidence that societies that historically surrounded people with highly visible and audible systems of timekeeping also developed strong cultural norms surrounding time?

Perhaps.

Correlation is certainly not causation, and I would not want to turn a summer observation into a grand theory of European culture.

But it raises an intriguing psychological possibility.

Maybe culture isn't only something we teach one another.

Maybe it is also embedded in the things we build around us.

What Is Your Environment Teaching You?

When I finally left Austria, I found myself thinking less about church bells and more about the invisible cues in my own environment.

Today, most of us no longer need a church tower to tell us that 15 minutes have passed. We carry something far more persistent in our pockets.

Our phones display the time. Our calendars alert us that a meeting begins in 10 minutes. Our watches vibrate. Our computers remind us of deadlines. Apps tell us how long until the car arrives, the food comes, or the package reaches our door.

In some ways, we have created our own digital church bells.

And perhaps that deserves more attention.

Because the way we experience time may not simply reflect our personality or culture. It may also reflect the environments we have created—and the cues those environments send us hundreds of times each day.

The church bells of Vienna and Salzburg reminded me of something surprisingly easy to forget:

We create tools to help us manage time. But eventually, those tools may begin to shape how we experience time itself.

item.title: The Trouble With “I Could Have Been Lindsay”
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

The Trouble With “I Could Have Been Lindsay”

Treating Lindsay Clancy with empathy doesn't necessitate recasting her as the victim.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Lindsay Clancy had a state of mind vanishingly few will ever know. Yet she has become a cause célèbre.
  • Postpartum depression affects roughly 1 in 7 mothers; postpartum psychosis is extremely uncommon.
  • Filicide by mothers with postpartum psychosis remains extremely rare even within an already rare condition.
  • Compassion doesn't require Clancy to be recast as the victim.

The murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, a woman who killed her three young children, has set off nationwide discussions not just about postpartum psychosis, but about the suffering of mothers more broadly and how the mental health system treats women. For some, Clancy has become a cause célèbre.

At a rally of hundreds outside the Massachusetts courthouse where Clancy is on trial, a 52-year-old paralegal from Providence, Rhode Island told a reporter that “women are being dismissed, neglected and ignored.” On X (formerly Twitter), Republican pundit Tiffany 😀 tweeted, “Our healthcare system has failed women.” One of dozens of letters of support in court documents came from a coworker of Clancy’s, a nurse who wrote, “I could have been Lindsay. Anyone of us could have been.”

Is this really true?

The defense argues that when Clancy killed her children, she had bipolar disorder with postpartum psychosis. On the night of the murders, they maintain, she experienced “command hallucinations” and “a delusion of influence.” As forensic psychiatrist Phillip Resnick explained, this means she not only heard a voice telling her what to do, she felt that her body had been “taken over by an external force… almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings.”

Unlike postpartum depression, which is a mood disorder that by some estimates affects about one in seven women, postpartum psychosis is an extremely rare psychiatric emergency thought to occur in roughly one to two women out of a thousand. Even fewer experience both command hallucinations and delusions of influence. And filicide is exceptionally uncommon. According to one study, 4.5 percent of women with postpartum psychosis kill their children.

It's perhaps strange, then, that Clancy has become a kind of everywoman.

“Motherhood will invariably introduce us to the less familiar, deeper strata of our humanity,” writes Jungian analyst Lisa Marchiano in her book, Motherhood, “where we are capable of the most destructive and reprehensible of acts.” Although the vast majority of mothers never harm their children, she writes, “most of us will admit in our more honest moments that we can at least imagine having those feelings, if only momentarily.”

Psychologist Doug Novotny points to 20th-century British psychoanalyst D.W. Winnicott’s theory of the “good enough mother,” whose imperfections are necessary for children’s psychological growth. The existence of ugly and even frightening maternal feelings is entirely consistent with being a good enough mother. (Acting on them, however, is not.)

In contrast, cognitive-behavioral psychologist Nando Pelusi suggests that solidarity with Clancy looks like what he calls coalition signaling. “Saying, ‘that could have been me’ is not really saying ‘I might have done this,’ but more, ‘I’m on her side against the system that failed her.’”

Perhaps this is how Clancy is transformed from the agent in the story into merely a victim in the eyes of many observers. The true agent, the villain, is the healthcare system; the mental health system; Big Pharma; the patriarchy. There is an assumption, generally coming from a place of empathy, that a woman who was so broken as to kill her own children must first have been victimized.

Whatever the reason that women see themselves in Lindsay Clancy, the likelihood that new mothers who suffer from sleep deprivation, isolation, or even postpartum depression actually understand the state of mind in which a mother strangles her own children is vanishingly low. They do, however, understand what it means to suffer. That focus may generate a kind of boundary-blurring empathy that produces their sense of identification with Clancy.

Ironically, this may be what some of Clancy’s supporters genuinely have in common with her. According to the prosecution’s theory, Clancy’s plan was what forensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun called “suicide combined with altruistic filicide.” She wanted to die but did not want her children to suffer without her, so she killed them believing they would always be together. In this view, Clancy’s own inability to imagine her children as psychologically separate from her helped produce her catastrophic conclusion that since she was determined to die, they would prefer to die, too.

Her supporters are not doing anything remotely comparable. But in collapsing the distance between themselves and Clancy, they make a related conceptual mistake: They substitute what they have felt or what they can imagine feeling for what she actually felt.

No matter which side is right about why, Lindsay Clancy is alive without her children, and she killed them. That must be a source of tremendous suffering for her. By all accounts, she was “a very loving mother who cared about her children,” as one of her children’s teachers described her. According to her mother-in-law, “She was very nurturing, very loving. She was a wonderful mother. Wonderful.” No witness has testified otherwise.

The jury is now deliberating. If convicted of first-degree murder, Clancy, who is permanently paralyzed from the waist down, will spend the rest of her life in prison with no possibility of parole. If convicted of murder in the second degree, the sentence is the same but parole is possible. If the jury returns a verdict of manslaughter, she will face up to 20 years in prison with the possibility of parole. And if she is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she will be committed to a secure state mental health facility—indefinitely, with release uncertain, and only under strict conditions.

None of those verdicts requires withholding compassion. Suffering and agency are not mutually exclusive. And agency need not preclude compassion. Neither does compassion require seeing Clancy as the victim in this story.

The victims were Cora (5), Dawson (3), and Callan (8 months).

item.title: Does Writing Letters Build Character?
item.description:
Social Life

Does Writing Letters Build Character?

Personal Perspective: Letter-writing fuels empathy, creativity, and literacy.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Our ancestors declared love and announced births and deaths in forms that took months to arrive.
  • Letter-writing cultivates empathy, patience, and risk-taking absent in instant messaging.
  • Handwritten letters are acts of faith, requiring courage and exposing writers to vulnerability.

We hardly ever say “mail” anymore.

That word implies archaic practices and products: stamps, pens, paper, and calling others “dear.”

Today we correspond faster than it takes to say “correspond,” typing in code to make it even faster.

MU, HRU

GR8, GTG

Even email feels obsolete.

As a child, I waited, frenzied, for our daily mail. The very theory of mail obsessed me: It linked people miles apart. So did phones, but written words seemed more sacred, transforming blank paper into bulletins: This is a craft. Trusting strangers to carry and deliver these: This is an act of faith.

We were taught letter-writing in third grade, where each student was assigned a faraway business to which we must write, seeking responses. I wrote to a tractor manufacturer.

Starting letters, even to strangers, with “dear,” and signing off after “love” or “yours truly,” did not seem bizarre. Yet it turned each missive, semantically at least, into an act of love.

The fifth-century chronicler Hellanicus of Lesbos credited Persia’s Queen Atossa with writing the first-ever letter in 500 BCE, although no trace of it remains.

How radical such contact must have felt back then, although at first permitted only to the privileged literate and whoever could hire scribes.

I pictured people wearing togas, tunics, mu’umu’us and kimonos, writing by torchlight and starlight in castles and trenches about crossbows, leprosy, and saints.

Handwritten correspondence fuels its own psychology because each card or letter is a social interaction, an engagement with an unpredictable response, protracted and projected over time and space.

Thus letter-writing is a risk. Even if said letter is only a shopping list, its composition and dispatch require effort, courage, and expense, exposing its sender to possible misunderstanding, mockery, or silence and the pain of wondering, perhaps forever, whether it arrived.

Sent letters make us wait. They force us to stay patient and unsure, imagining ten thousand possible responses, with twenty thousand suspended hopes and fears.

For anyone who expects instant gratification, this would be hell.

At twelve, I planned to someday be an avid adult correspondent, dispatching the latest news with insightful analysis on seahorse stationery in that slanting script we’d learned at school.

I understood only subconsciously that letter-writing was — for we who loathed ourselves, who were not beautiful, whose parents called us pigs — a precious way in which to possibly be liked.

It is a kind of grace: a still caesura in which to practice, unseen, our powers of description, consolation, and persuasion, and choose stamps, stickers, and sealing wax to best suit each recipient. Each card and letter is a gift.

Reading the works of famous correspondents whose letters were archived — Erich Maria Rilke, for instance — my young self wanted to join them.

History had other plans.

Who could have dreamed that correspondence would become easy and instantaneous? Who could have dreamed that replies would arrive within a breath?

Who could have dreamed that, although private correspondence still exists, the vast majority would become public: chats, streams, social media, and other apps where countless strangers worldwide join, shape, doom, and even dominate our dialogues.

It’s fast. It’s often fun, but sometimes scary. It can end careers in microseconds.

And, for all its ease, is modern correspondence erasing — or never teaching anyone to start with — crucial mental skills built into old-skool correspondence? Texting fuels neither eloquence nor patience nor the power to survive suspense. Chatting on streams and social media prioritizes neither privacy nor intimacy but performativity. Anonymous communication lets us be guiltlessly crueler than old-fashioned correspondence ever did.

Does posting puke emojis systematically render us less polite? When we no longer start and end our messages with “dear” and “love,” however formulaic that once was, are we becoming cold?

Or does current-day correspondence build positive skills? Do instant messaging and rapid responses render us confident and calm and better able to swiftly articulate our thoughts?

Had you told our ancestors, “Someday, people will correspond instantly, like this” — tapping in pantomime — “and even send each other pictures, videos and sound,” they would have queried, “What are videos?” then stood there stunned as you explained.

Our ancestors in their corsets and kilts would ask us how and when. They’d think of twenty thousand things to tell their partners, parents, and those friends they left behind in Abyssinia. The very thought of those missives arriving instantly would feel miraculous, like actually being gods.

item.title: Forced Psychiatric Treatment Is Supposed to Be a Last Resort
item.description:
Law and Crime

Forced Psychiatric Treatment Is Supposed to Be a Last Resort

A new report suggests that New York City is overusing Assisted Outpatient Treatment.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • New report finds that intensive voluntary treatment achieves results similar to court-ordered treatment.
  • New York law allows involuntary outpatient treatment only if no less restrictive option is available.
  • New York City appears to be using court-mandated treatment too often and not as a last resort.

Courts in nearly every state have the authority to mandate outpatient treatment for certain individuals with mental illness who have been unwilling or unable to access needed treatment voluntarily. It’s called “Assisted Outpatient Treatment” (or “AOT”).

With Kendra’s Law in 1999, New York State was at the forefront of the national movement to adopt AOT. The policy was controversial then and remains controversial today. Both supporters and opponents are now citing a new, 392-page independent evaluation of AOT in New York. The report compared AOT with a comparable, but voluntary, intensive outpatient program called “Assertive Community Treatment” (or “ACT”).

The Controversy Continues

Supporters of AOT focus on the study’s quantitative results. The executive summary lists four outcomes where AOT did significantly better than ACT, two outcomes where ACT did significantly better, and four with no statistically significant differences (exhibit 1, page 3).

Notably absent from the executive summary is one of the primary justifications for AOT, medication adherence, where voluntary ACT did significantly better (exhibit 4.26, page 177). There were no significant differences between AOT and ACT on three other key outcomes also not listed in the summary: risk of harm to self, support needed for independent living, and employment.

AOT skeptics, including an author of the study, argue that the quantitative findings are being misinterpreted. For example, even though AOT improved housing by a greater statistical margin than ACT, ACT improved housing outcomes for many more people than AOT.

Gavel poised to strike
Source: KATRIN BOLOVTSOVA / Pexels

For those keeping score, dropping the disputed housing outcome and adding medication adherence to the list of key outcomes would result in a three-to-three tie between AOT and voluntary ACT, plus many more outcomes with no statistically significant differences.

But the main criticism of AOT, based on qualitative data, is that many participants feel confused, coerced, and powerless. These real costs should break the tie in favor of voluntary ACT, the argument goes. The law agrees.

Least Restrictive Alternative

Under New York statute, a court is authorized to order AOT only if “there is no appropriate and feasible less restrictive alternative.” It doesn’t take qualitative data to recognize that a voluntary program is less restrictive than a mandatory one.

To be sure, the new report did not attempt to determine whether the “less restrictive alternative” requirement was met in any particular case, let alone in the thousands of cases included in the study. But the report includes enough data to suggest that New York City, which accounts for a very large share of AOT orders statewide, is not meeting this legal requirement.

New York City Exceptionalism

NYC courthouse
Source: 12019, Pixabay

First, there is woefully inadequate access in NYC to voluntary ACT, which the quantitative data discussed above shows could be a viable less restrictive option than AOT. Specifically, the wait time in NYC for ACT without an AOT order is over two years (table 3a, page 279). Voluntary ACT programs are more readily available in every other region of the state.

Second, NYC is the only region in the state in which courts never consider another less restrictive outpatient option before ordering AOT, the “Enhanced Voluntary Agreement” (or “EVA”) (table 13a, page 302). Voluntary pre-AOT diversion interventions have been shown to avoid the need for involuntary treatment for many individuals with serious mental illness.

A final piece of data in the report supports the conclusion that NYC is overusing AOT: the city has far fewer significant negative events among AOT participants than any other region (exhibit 4.23, page 172). Sure, it’s possible that the AOT program in the city is better than AOT elsewhere in the state, but a more plausible explanation is that a higher percentage of AOT participants in NYC would have avoided bad outcomes without the force of a court order.

Conclusion

No single study will resolve the long-running and heated controversy over AOT. But the recent report strongly suggests that NYC is not providing, or even considering, some voluntary alternatives to AOT that are used successfully elsewhere in the state. Forced psychiatric treatment is supposed to be a last resort. At least in NYC, it does not appear to be.

item.title: When Praising Is Processed as Pressure and Backfires
item.description:
Parenting

When Praising Is Processed as Pressure and Backfires

Consider these strategies for nurturing self-confidence and engaging cooperation

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Kids may reject praise when it's processed as evaluation of their performance. It makes them self-conscious.
  • Some kids process praise is a method for control, to get them to cooperate. This can engage their defiance.
  • One fix is to shift from praise to process, and to stop calling attention to a child's compliance.

The message most parents get about praise is that it’s critical for building kids’ self-esteem and for showing them that their accomplishments are seen and valued.

We’re also led to believe that when we tell our kids how proud we are when they finally poop on the potty, or agree to try a new food or activity, or perform at a sporting event or recital, that praise will reinforce that behavior. That it’s Pavlovian: heap on the praise and your child will do more of whatever you are applauding.

But what happens when praise has the opposite effect? When your child rejects it: they demand you stop talking when you are praising them to other people, or they tell you not to say “Good job” or clap when they have performed well or have followed through on a task. They may even do a complete about-face. You tell them how glad you are that they are trying a new food, and they promptly spit it out. You tell them how proud you are that they are wearing underwear, and they go back to demanding pull-ups.

When kids reject praise, there may be several underlying issues at play:

They’re self-conscious and don’t like people calling attention to them

They may process praise as pressure and feel like you’re evaluating their performance—which, in fact, you are. This can be stifling, not motivating, for kids. The flipside of praise is disappointment. You praise their goal in soccer, so in their next competition, if they don’t score, they worry they’re letting you down.

Kids perceive that praise as a tool for control, which, in fact, it is

We praise the behaviors we want to see more of, and they know it. For the kids who are wired to be heat-seeking missiles for power and control, praise effectively means they have caved to your agenda or authority, which is totally anathema to them. These kids prioritize power over everything and do not want the optics to be that you have “won.”

I met with a family who has been trying to get their 4-year-old to poop on the potty for a year, offering endless praise and incentives. Then they found residual toilet paper in his underwear after school (the teacher confirmed he has been using the potty at school), and their caregiver told them that he has pooped on the potty with her, but dictates, “Don’t tell Mommy or Daddy.”

Another family reported that one night they held firm on not giving their child the chicken nuggets he demanded, nor did they react to his threats that he wouldn’t eat anything else and would thus starve. They later found him in his room eating the grilled chicken and carrots he had apparently taken from the table. Why would a child do that? So as not to give his parents the satisfaction that he had acquiesced to their limit. These kids will not eat crow! (No pun intended.)

Addressing these challenges requires suspending logic (Why wouldn’t my child want to see how proud we are of him?) and not taking one-size-fits-all guidance as gospel.

Here are some strategies that can support your child’s positive sense of self and engage their cooperation:

Don’t call attention to your child’s acquiescence

Say you hold the limit that you’re not making chicken nuggets for dinner. Your child ultimately comes to the table and starts nibbling at the food on offer. Don’t say a word about it, à la, “You’re making such a good choice to eat growing foods!” Just integrate them into the dinner conversation to show you’re enjoying their company.

Don’t in any way show that you care a lick (no pun intended) about whether they eat or not. As counterintuitive as that may seem, it’s your caring (aka your agenda) that’s fodder for resistance—to prove they’re in charge.

What about if your child is self-conscious, doesn’t like attention, and processes praise as pressure?

What if your child worries that you’re evaluating their performance, which can lead to a fear of failure? Or, when heaping praise is making your child dependent on external validation to feel worthy and valued, and is making them sore at losing, à la this story from one client:

“We thought we were building Rohan's self-esteem by praising everything he did: how smart, clever, and athletic he is. But now, at 5, he has all this bravado, and he’s a braggart. I feel terrible saying this, but he’s become an obnoxious know-it-all who constantly needs to top others, which is not working so well with his friends. If a child makes two goals, he’ll say he made four, which is just not true. If someone shares a fact, say, about dinosaurs, he counters, ‘I know the most about dinosaurs.’ He’s also become a very sore loser. Now we’re not sure what to do. Seems our approach backfired.”

These suggestions can help:

  • Don’t talk to others about your child in front of them, especially if you want to brag about them. It can feel intrusive and overwhelming to see how much you care about their performance.
  • Change your focus from praise to process. Comment on the impact of their effort on them, not its impact on you: “You worked so hard to keep your eye on the ball, which helped you get that goal. I can see how good that makes you feel.” Versus, “You made a goal! We’re so proud of you! You’re the best soccer player!”
  • Communicate that what’s important to you is not their performance, but seeing them experience pleasure in whatever they’re doing.
  • As tempting as it may be, don’t manipulate it so your child always wins when playing games. That’s not how the real world works, so it’s a missed opportunity for them to experience that they can survive not being the winner. Think: “I love playing catch with you. But when you shout at me or want to change the rules, it’s not fun for me. So we can have a redo and keep playing, which I would love, or we can move on to something else.”
  • Explain that they are still smart and valued, even when others—friends, siblings, etc.—get the right answer or win a game (AKA, comparison is the thief of joy!).
  • Validate how hard it feels to not be the best or the winner, but that it’s going to happen, given that we’re human. Share how you learned to manage those difficult moments so that you could be a good teammate and enjoy, not be stressed by, competition, which makes it no fun. Brainstorm strategies to help your child stay calm and cope when they’re in these triggering situations.
  • Show your child video clips of people they admire—like Messi—having a bad game. Explain that it doesn’t define him, and that even pro athletes have to keep working on their skills. Then there was the family who shared clips of John McEnroe throwing tantrums to show how uncomfortable his behavior makes others feel. That was also very effective!

It’s all about using what you know about your child—what makes them tick—to wonder why praise would make them uncomfortable and backfire. That’s what gives you the insight into how to respond in a way that is most sensitive and effective.

item.title: Mindful Use of Yoga Matters in Eating Disorder Recovery
item.description:
Eating Disorders

Mindful Use of Yoga Matters in Eating Disorder Recovery

Yoga found to be promising for eating disorder prevention and treatment.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Yoga can support eating disorder recovery by improving body image, self-compassion, and emotional regulation.
  • Fitness-focused yoga may reinforce perfectionism, body criticism, and unhealthy exercise or eating behaviors.
  • Trauma-informed yoga promotes safety and body acceptance instead of focusing on appearance or performance.
  • Gentle yoga can support early recovery by helping people reconnect with their bodies.

This post was written jointly by Ruby Kagan and Robert T. Muller, Ph.D.

A resurgence of thin-biased, toxic norms is fueling a new wave of body dissatisfaction, disordered eating, and a rising global prevalence of eating disorders. Eating disorders like anorexia nervosa are among the deadliest of all mental health conditions. Western treatments for eating disorders have traditionally prioritized nutritional rehabilitation and cognitive therapies.

Since 2005, a growing body of research supports the value of somatic approaches, like the practice of yoga, that treat the body as central to healing rather than merely a battleground. Carolyn Costin, author, clinician, and founder of the first residential treatment center to incorporate yoga into clinical care, describes yoga as a powerful tool “to concretize reconnecting mind, body, and soul.”

A 2020 study found yoga to be promising for eating disorder prevention and treatment, suggesting that it reduced disordered eating behaviors and enhanced body image, emotional regulation, and re-embodiment. The researchers noted the importance of cultivating positive rather than negative embodiment, which accepts the body as it is as opposed to viewing it as defective and in need of change.

Source: Mikhail Nilov / Pexels

Similarly, a 2025 study backs up the value of somatic approaches, finding that participants in a structured yoga program showed statistically significant improvements in eating disorder symptoms, body appreciation, self-care, self-compassion, and interoceptive awareness.

The relationship between yoga and eating disorders is complex, and even Costin, who pioneered and advocates strongly, acknowledges that yoga can be harmful if misapplied. For some, yoga is the beginning of reclaiming and accepting their bodies. For others, it simply reinforces an unhealthy cycle of self-criticism and over-control.

In 8 Keys to Recovery from an Eating Disorder, Costin discusses how common traits among those with eating disorders, such as anxiety, perfectionism, and compulsivity, can undermine restorative somatic practices. She cautions that yoga without mindful guidance can become “just another area in which to strive for perfection,” rather than a space for healing and self-acceptance.

As the practice has surged in popularity, it has also been increasingly co-opted by diet culture and aesthetic obsessions. Instagram images of hyper-toned bodies in acrobatic poses, or class language that emphasizes calorie burning, can reinforce unhealthy, overly appearance-focused thinking.

Yoga, like many well-intentioned practices, can be corrupted. Costin has seen “very driven and competitive people injure themselves mimicking the teacher, or excessively engaging in fasting, juice cleanses, and raw food diets.” When the practice is too fitness-oriented, it can become about who’s doing the most backbends or burning the most calories.

Source: Yan Krukau / Pexels

According to eating disorder expert Anita Federici, common weight- and body-centric language in such environments can lower self-esteem, reduce body satisfaction, and worsen eating disorder symptoms. Federici values the use of yoga for eating disorder recovery, but also worries that the wrong messaging and intentionality can exacerbate obsessions with physique, flexibility, or strength.

Unfortunately, many yoga teacher training programs offer minimal education on trauma and eating disorders. This lack of awareness can lead to unintended harms, such as language that reinforces body monitoring, criticism, or perfectionism. However, the growing movement of trauma-informed yoga emphasizes autonomy, choice, and emotional safety. Teachers of this approach are trained to avoid physical adjustments, eliminate triggering language, and offer options rather than commands. The solution isn’t to abandon yoga for eating disorders, but to be more mindful of its use and delivery.

Costin offers more active practices for those physically able, alongside restful alternatives for those in more fragile states. Inclusivity is emphasized, as even clients too underweight to engage in typical yoga sessions can participate lying down with a lavender mask. Teachers also integrate body-positive affirmations and reflective practices. Journaling is a key element in Costin’s approach: “I like to get people to write things down to talk back to the disordered part. Writing retrains the brain and makes it real.”

For individuals in early recovery, slower, breath-based practices, like yin or restorative yoga, are often more appropriate than fast-paced, fitness-oriented flows. These gentler styles support nervous system regulation and embodied awareness without mimicking compulsive exercise.

Federici emphasizes a staged approach: “In the beginning, we often recommend avoiding heated rooms, mirrors, or physically intense classes. It’s about learning to be in your body, not push it.” Recovery, she says, is best served by honoring yoga’s cultural roots that extend beyond over-prioritizing physical poses (asanas).

To realize yoga’s substantial healing potential, the when, how, and why it is practiced matters. Yoga can be an effective adjunct to evidence-based therapies, warranting greater inclusion in treatment toolkits and settings. When practiced with humility, trauma awareness, and philosophical grounding, yoga becomes an invaluable resource to help reclaim the self, reinhabit the body, and restore hope. According to Costin, becoming “fully recovered” is a goal never beyond reach.

item.title: The Last Room Without a Camera
item.description:
Neuroscience

The Last Room Without a Camera

Brain-monitoring devices are entering the workplace faster than rules to govern them.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Our thoughts are the last space where we can say anything without consequence.
  • We may need to protect mental privacy before the technology settles the question for us.
  • What happens to the last unmonitored space when monitoring becomes wearable?
  • Rights are rarely taken all at once. They are stepped away from.

The most frequent cognitive activity of humans is self-talk (see Alderson-Day & Fernyhough, 2015). Almost 24/7, we talk to ourselves. This is not a pathological tendency, per se, but like any other tendency, it can turn out to be pathological. However, one of the beauties of self-talk is its privacy. Within our brain-walls we can say what we want without fear of repercussion. You can raise your voice against the powerful, you can yell at your condescending boss, or say to your colleague whatever you wanted to say for a long time.

Yet, what was once confined to clinical trials is now entering the mainstream. Cutting-edge neurotechnologies—like wearable EEG headsets that track vigilance and exhaustion—are rapidly being integrated into modern workplaces, bringing brain science directly into the nine-to-five grind (Muhl & Andorno, 2023). At the same time, consumer-grade EEG headsets are being sold to corporate offices, training programs, and wellness initiatives with claims that they can measure concentration, alertness, and mood (Wexler & Reiner, 2019).

We have learned, the hard way, that invasion of privacy and human rights violations do not happen overnight. They are gradual and normally start with small steps. The journey from asking a few volunteers to wear a headset to mandating one for all workers is only as long as our willingness to look the other way.

For virtually all of human history, we have possessed one place in which our freedom was absolute: inside our own minds. We should decide whether that boundary matters before technology decides for us. Maybe we need to add a few paragraphs to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and protect our neuro rights (United Nations, 1948; UNESCO, 2025).
