item.title: What Else Makes a Laughter Theory Comprehensive?
item.description:
Laughter

What Else Makes a Laughter Theory Comprehensive?

A dozen more topics a full description of laughter and humor must address.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Scholars attempting to understand why we laugh have failed to develop a single, complete theory.
  • Problems are often the result of diverse causal factors and consequences associated with this behavior.
  • Here I briefly describe some topics scholars address as they attempt to comprehend this enigmatic behavior.

In my last post, I shared some findings from an article titled “Essential Attributes of a Comprehensive Theory of Laughter” (Simon, 2020), which listed topics raised by modern laughter scholars in their peer-reviewed writings. I wanted to expose some of the difficulties investigators face when attempting to develop a single “unified” laughter theory, one capable of answering all the questions raised, some going back as far as Ancient Greece (Halliwell, 2008). Unfortunately, I had space to cover only about a third of the issues interested theorists must address, so here I’d like to add a few more examples.

Previously reported themes

Last month’s article covered these themes: the physiological basis of atypical laughter behaviors as they relate to various cognitive or emotional disabilities; the social consequences of laughter and humor, both positive and negative; precisely where in the brain laughter is initiated; what physical benefits, if any, laughter provides to the individual expressing it; how laughter and humor may help us cope with difficult circumstances; explaining the tremendous variation we see in people’s laugh response; laughter’s relationship to humor; the essential role or function laughter’s has in an evolutionary sense; and why we sometimes misinterpret the sentiments behind others’ laughter. Listed below are the next most common themes encountered during my search.

Source: Jonathan Borba / Pexels

More subjects the experts have raised

Acoustic Structure: Whether or not one assumes laughter is a form of nonverbal communication, a complete theory should be able to explain why, among all the other options available, laughter has the vocal signature it does. For that matter, why is it a vocalization at all rather than some other physiological reaction, such as puffing out one’s cheeks or pulling on an earlobe?

Message Conveyed: If a theorist presupposes laughter as being some form of communication, what message or messages does it convey? If it has more than one message, what method or markers are used to differentiate them?

Indicators of Personality, Health, and Status: It is generally held that people glean information about others’ personality (e.g., extroversion), physical and/or emotional health (e.g., depression), and their social status (e.g., acquiescence) from their laugh response…or lack thereof. What are the traits people associate with laughter, and how reliable are the inferences people make?

Laughter’s Relationship With Smiling: There is a clear link between laughter and smiling. We often smile before beginning a bout of sincere laughter and almost always follow such laughter with a smile. Is this coincidental, or is there some overlap in the motivations behind, or meaning of, these two behaviors?

Laughter’s Dual Nature: It’s not quite universal, but most cultures appear to differentiate between at least two “types” of laughter. One form is associated with friendly, supportive emotions (i.e., laughing “with” others) and a second form is linked with feelings of condescension and even malice (i.e., laughing “at” others). Why do these two internal motivations share a single outward form? Why not simply evolve two clearly different expressions, one gracious and the other antagonistic?

Source: BSM Rental / Pexels

Origins: No theory of laughter would be complete without a plausible account of its evolutionary origins. When did laughter originate in our evolutionary history and from what source or “parent” behavior? Do the similar (but not vocally identical) expressions used by orangutans, gorillas, bonobos, and chimpanzees serve the same function as that proposed for humans? What about other, more distantly related species? Do any have a comparable behavior?

Volitional Laughter: Most of us have, at various times, felt compelled to laugh even absent the feeling of amusement. We might feign laughter if we think others expect (or at least hope) for us to respond in that way. Or we might fake a bout of laughter in a sarcastic way to suggest something isn’t funny. Why would we pretend to laugh, particularly if a theory presupposes laughter did not evolve to convey a message?

Contagiousness: It has been well established that laughter is often, but not always, contagious. That is, a person’s laughter itself generates feelings of amusement and laughter in others. Why would it spread from person to person in this way? Why might it not? What factors are at play?

Varieties: More than a few scholars have suggested there are different kinds of laughter—nervous laughter, joyous laughter, malicious laughter, embarrassed laughter, elevating laughter, etc. Does each serve a separate physiological function or convey a different message? Or is this a case of many different motivations all being responsible for a singular action?

Variations in Intensity or Duration: Laugh responses come in many degrees. It can be an almost imperceptible nasal “snort,” a single chuckle, a gentle giggle lasting a few seconds, a hearty guffaw, all the way up to a fall-on-the-floor “roller” that might go on for minutes. Why do bouts of laughter vary so much in intensity and duration? What influences our response to a particular stimulus?

Laughter and Humor’s Use by Bullies: The laughter of others is often, but not always, welcomed. There seems to be a relationship between it and bullying behavior. How does one explain laughter as a means of defamation, belittlement, and scorn? What are the motivations behind the use of antagonistic humor?

Source: Andres Ayrton / Pexels

Relationship to Tickling: There is a clear link between laughter and tickling, at least for those who are “ticklish.” What is it about being tickled that explains the seemingly uncontrolled expression of laughter in some individuals while generating little or no effect in others? Why is it virtually impossible for even highly susceptible people to tickle themselves into a bout of sincere laughter?

The increasing scope

Combined with last month’s list, the themes enumerated here make it increasingly clear that any comprehensive explanation of the enigmatic behavior we call laughter must ultimately take into account dozens of wide-ranging issues.

I’ll present the final collection of examples, and a few additional thoughts, in next month’s post.

item.title: Swing Away at Life
item.description:
Self-Help

Swing Away at Life

Say yes to life and make it meaningful.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Your mindset will determine whether or not you will be able to cope with what life throws at you.
  • You always have the freedom to choose your attitude when facing life challenges.
  • It’s your choice to watch life pass by or actively engage with it.
  • Swing away at your life by committing to meaningful values and goals.
Source: Darunrat Wongsuvan / Shutterstock

Recently, I had the opportunity to reconnect with my dear friend, George E. Stephanopoulos, an entertainment attorney and the producer and writer of the 2017 comedy film Swing Away. The film is about a pro golfer who, after a suspension from playing in tour events, escapes to her grandparents’ village in Greece to reflect upon the deeper meaning of her life. I was honored to serve as a consulting producer on this exciting film project.

The title of the movie is significant not only because it is a common golf term, meaning to hit the ball with ease and freedom, but also because it is a metaphor for living a full and authentic life. It is the latter interpretation of the term that can be seen as a guidepost for discovering meaning in everyday life.

Many of us use sports metaphors to capture the nuances of daily living. Yet there appears to be something very special about “golf” and what it mirrors about the human condition.

In his 1971 bestselling novel Golf in the Kingdom, for example, Michael Murphy, a co-founder of the Esalen Institute and a key figure in the human potential movement, explored the deeper meaning and metaphysical dimensions of golf. Much like the mystical caddy in the 2000 American sports fantasy drama The Legend of Bagger Vance, a young man (modeled on the author) stumbles upon a mysterious Zen Master-like golf pro, Shivas Irons, who over a 24-hour period teaches him important lessons about golf, spirituality, and the meaning of life. As a result, the young Murphy character experiences an unexpected personal transformation; he discovers his “inner body” and becomes aware that, metaphorically speaking, there was already a perfect golf swing inside him.

Like other films in its genre, Swing Away is not really a movie about golf per se. Rather, it is a movie about life, about experiencing the joy of living, regardless of one’s personal circumstances, and about embracing all of life—the joys and sorrows, the ups and downs—with attitude.1

Although we may not always have control over the circumstances within which we find ourselves, we always have the ultimate freedom to choose how we will respond to them, even if only through our choice of attitude.2 As human beings, we have the inherent benefits of creativity, reason, and faith that, to one degree or another, stand ready to help us answer life’s call for meaning in all situations.

And because we are human, we have the added benefit of enjoying and discovering the deeper meaning of our journey. This is why it is important metaphorically to not give up, to keep trying, and to “swing away” at life by committing to living to the fullest.

Speaking both philosophically and metaphysically, George Stephanopoulos underscored the deeper meaning behind his writing the script for Swing Away:

“It also serves as a metaphor that expresses the idea that it’s only in following the yearnings and dreams of one’s true self or in rediscovering them that allows people, the universe, or even the golf gods in this case, to bring joy and unity into our lives. And it’s only through comedy that this theme can be adequately expressed in a way that reminds each of us to let go of the things holding us back and ‘swing away’ in our own lives.”

When asked what he wanted audiences to get from watching Swing Away, George was quite clear: “I want audiences to be inspired, to laugh and to experience the joy in living life to its fullest. Of course, we want people to be entertained and have not only a wonderful movie-going experience, but to come away with a greater understanding of Greece as a whole, as well as the unique spirit and passion of the Greek people. Most importantly, at the end of the day, we want people to walk out of the theater feeling happy, inspired, and free to live their dreams.”

When we search out and discover the authentic meaning of our existence and our experiences, we learn that life doesn’t just happen to us. We happen to life, and we make it meaningful. Indeed, meaning exists in each moment of life, even as the world-renowned psychiatrist and Holocaust survivor Dr. Viktor E. Frankl famously espoused, “in the most miserable situations and literally up to the last breadth of ourselves.”

Dr. Frankl’s ageless wisdom provides a beacon of hope for humanity even in what may be dark times. Consistent with his meaning-focused, extraordinary life and legacy, he certainly practiced what he preached when he advised people to say yes to life, in spite of everything!3 Put differently, no matter what happens to you, remember to keep making the effort, keep taking chances, and “swing away” at life.

item.title: Overcoming Emotional Inertia: How to Let Go of a Feeling
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

Overcoming Emotional Inertia: How to Let Go of a Feeling

Dealing with emotional inertia is an essential skill for emotional regulation.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional inertia entails being susceptible to loops of emotions or moods that are difficult to shake loose.
  • While emotional inertia can refer to negative or positive emotions, it more often involves negative emotions.
  • Early trauma is often associated with emotional inertia, as it creates a sensitivity to being triggered.
  • Moving past emotional inertia begins with recognizing its occurrence and building skills in self-soothing.

A ’70s song titled “I’m Hooked on a Feeling” highlights the fixation on a feeling of love that can even be addictive. This is an example of “emotional inertia”: being susceptible to loops of emotions or moods that are difficult to shake. And being able to let go of emotions is a key skill for emotional regulation.

Emotional inertia may also be defined as the resistance to emotional change (Kuppens, Allen, & Sheeber, 2010). A high degree of emotional inertia reflects a fixation on one’s inner landscape, in contrast to attending to the details of one’s environment (Kuppens, Sheeba, Yap, et. al., 2012). This may be reflected within an hour, a day, or a lifetime.

While emotional inertia may involve positive feelings such as love, it more often entails negative emotions related to a predisposition and sensitivity to become emotionally triggered. Such difficulty has been found to be associated with depression, esteem issues, and fear of negative evaluation. I’ve observed this in some clients who reported having few memories of certain periods in their lives. This is a consequence of their preoccupation with their internal reactivity to the exclusion of what was occurring around them.

Some clients have described their reactions to stressful events that occurred in the morning, leaving them wishing for the end of the day—as if they could only escape such moods through the dawning of a new day. This is an example of emotional inertia supported by difficulties in flexibility and emotional regulation in general.

Letting go of an unhelpful mood
Source: Alexan 107 / 123rf

Links to Emotional Inertia

Emotional inertia often results from trauma that serves as an imprint for future experiences. Not letting go of and effectively dealing with such trauma contributes to the mind-body set that is uncomfortable with letting go of certain emotions. In effect, the brain learns to be on high alert for potential harm and has difficulty letting go of such hypervigilance. While originating in an effort to protect oneself, such inertia prevents an individual from both taking in and savoring the good. This is consistent with research that has found that negative emotional inertia occurs much more frequently than positive emotional inertia.

Further research has suggested that emotional inertia for negative emotions (negative emotional inertia) may be an indicator of a greater vulnerability to depression (Koval, Sutterlin, and Kuppens, 2016). Exhaustion has also been found to contribute to emotional inertia (Alessandri, De Longis, and Cepale, 2021). This is consistent with findings that cognitive alertness decreases flexibility of thinking.

With regard to intimate relationships, research has shown that partners of individuals with high emotional inertia experienced their partner as being less responsive to their emotions (Tamara and Schoebi, 2019). The preoccupation with emotional inertia leaves the partner less available to take in information, even when it may help challenge the inertia. As such, their tendency for negative emotion was associated with a greater undermining of the quality of the relationship.

Strategies to Address Emotional Inertia

As with establishing any new habit related to emotional regulation, reducing the tendency toward emotional inertia entails developing skills in self-observation and self-monitoring to recognize patterns in one’s behavior and emotions. Consistent with all aspects of my clinical work, I’ve always encouraged clients to practice such monitoring by taking a brief break to attend to their “mind-body” states several times daily. This can strengthen attention to self-awareness of emotions and thoughts. Writing notes or using apps for self-monitoring strengthens self-awareness. Certainly, this is a foundational aspect of mindfulness as well as a key capacity supported by mindfulness meditation.

When working with my clients, I emphasize that they become mindful of a sense of time and the openness of every moment to be different from the one that preceded it. So, for example, I suggest they practice viewing the day as consisting of numerous 15-minute periods and treat each new period as an opportunity to release attention from the previous one and choose to attend to the freshness of the new moment. This is supported by consciously immersing oneself in that moment.

A client with whom I worked described being preoccupied during her lunch hour by tension regarding her work. I suggested that, in order to be more present during her lunch hour, she immerse herself in the details of her environment through all of her senses—that she attend to sounds, fragrances, sights, and sensations as she heads out to lunch. When necessary, I encouraged her to make an appointment for a later moment and set aside a timed period to brainstorm rather than worry about her work.

Another approach I’ve recommended to clients who become preoccupied with the tension of the workday is to develop a “psychological mudroom.” I coined this term as a reference to the entryway of a house that is where you leave your dirty shoes, clothing, and outdoor gear. It serves to keep out dirt, mud, and clutter from the outside world.

By psychological mudroom, I refer to a ritual that might help people to mindfully let go of the difficult emotions of the day. Some may listen to music or an audiobook on the drive home or read a book on public transportation. Others may sit in the driveway or chill by going through a scenic road when possible. They may seek cooperation and support from loved ones to let them relax alone for several minutes in a room of their choice. These strategies may also help those who are tempted to use alcohol to cope at the end of the day.

Practicing the above strategies strengthens the capacity to be present in our lives. And with such presence comes the freedom to choose to focus on the positive, even when we may not have complete control over what unfolds throughout the day. It’s one thing to choose to set aside some time for brainstorming about an issue and another to have our moods and thoughts hijacked by the impact of some external triggering event.

Certainly, there are times when it might be helpful to take time to more fully reflect on other emotions associated with the current mood as well as past events that might make you more sensitive to being triggered. When this is the case, intentionally choose when and where you might do so. This stands in sharp contrast to having your moods evolve into emotional inertia. This often requires the hard work of making peace with the past. As such, seeking professional help can also assist you in developing the tools to overcome the tendency toward emotional inertia.

item.title: What Happens When You Stop Fighting Yourself
item.description:
Autism

What Happens When You Stop Fighting Yourself

Bianca Toeps on autism, diagnostic labels, and finding peace.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • A diagnostic label isn’t a limitation. For many autistic people, it’s a map.
  • Removing the autism label doesn’t remove the autism.
  • Autism looks different across cultures, but the debate is universal.
Understanding yourself isn't the same as limiting yourself.
Source: Bianca Toeps / Used with permission

“Fighting yourself can never lead to real progress, because you are yourself. You’re simply applying opposing forces to the same person. The result isn’t forward movement, it’s just exhaustion.”

Bianca Toeps explained it using physics. For me, it captures something important about what happens when someone spends years trying to overcome who they are instead of understanding themselves.

Bianca is the author of But You Don’t Look Autistic at All and This Autistic Girl Went to Japan, both translated into multiple languages. She was diagnosed with autism at 26, after years of burnout, an eating disorder, and the persistent feeling that she was letting everyone down. She is currently based in Japan, and she agreed to speak with me for this post following her recent essay on the debate over abolishing psychiatric diagnostic labels.

The Definition of “Car”

The debate over psychiatric diagnostic labels has been gaining attention. Jim van Os, a prominent Dutch psychiatrist, published a piece in Nature arguing against DSM-style diagnostic categories in favour of needs-based care. The proposal sounds reasonable. Bianca’s response focuses on something the broader debate can overlook: what happens to people who rely on diagnostic language to understand themselves.

“The problem is that removing the diagnostic label doesn’t remove the symptoms,” she tells me. “It’s not as if people will suddenly stop stigmatising my behaviour, or as if I’ll suddenly stop struggling with communication and sensory issues.”

She uses an analogy that is difficult to argue with. Imagine having to describe a car without using the word car: “A metal transportation vehicle that runs on fossil fuels and has four tyres.” Technically accurate, not particularly useful.

“Receiving an autism diagnosis gives people that kind of word,” she says. “It can be incredibly helpful when researching, reading books, or finding other people like you. It also helps prevent you from having to explain the same things over and over again.”

Without the label, she adds, people respond to descriptions of her sensory needs with “Oh, everybody has that, right? It can’t be that bad.” The word autism signals that it is more than that.

Before She Had a Diagnosis

Before the diagnosis, Bianca had a different theory about herself: She simply wasn’t trying hard enough. This is a common story among autistic women diagnosed late. She describes that period without self-pity, focusing instead on what she believed about herself at the time: “I felt like a disappointment. When I was a child, people told me I was gifted. And now I felt like I was letting everyone down. I started to hate myself. I developed an eating disorder and experienced multiple burnouts.”

After her diagnosis, she tried medication: a low-dose antipsychotic prescribed off-label for autistic people. It calmed her. It also made her less funny, and she enjoyed things less. “When I stopped taking it," she says, "I made a decision: This is who I am. I’m not going to medicate myself just to be more palatable to other people.”

After that, she made a series of practical changes to how she organized her life. She plans an empty day after every day with heavy social demands. She travels outside peak hours. She books first class when she knows a train journey will be overwhelming. When going to a party, she stays one or two hours and always ensures she can leave independently.

“The biggest change was learning from my own experiences,” she says. She started logging events in her planner after they happened, not just before. “Before that, I would often be surprised that I was completely exhausted after certain events. Once I started seeing the patterns, I learned to anticipate them.”

The Visible Outsider

Bianca has been following the label debate from Japan, where the social environment around autism is different. “Many parts of society are structured around clear rules and routines, making them relatively easy to navigate once you know the script,” she says. “Trains are usually quiet and reliable. It’s also quite normal to have hobbies or interests that you’re deeply invested in.”

But the expectations around reading social cues are intense, and the stigma around seeking help remains significant. She mentions hikikomori, the phenomenon of extreme social withdrawal, often rooted in untreated depression, anxiety, or autism, sustained by family shame rather than addressed.

For Bianca personally, being a foreigner offers an unexpected buffer. When she makes a social mistake, people attribute it to cultural difference rather than neurodivergence. She finds that oddly comforting.

“I’d much rather be a visible outsider here than an invisible outsider in the Netherlands, where people expect me to understand every social cue and unwritten rule.”

On Growing Into a Diagnosis

One criticism of diagnostic labels is that they can become a reason for people to stop pushing themselves. Bianca has thought about this carefully. “Time and time again, at book signings and speaking events, people have come up to me and told me that their diagnosis changed their lives for the better,” she says. “It gave them the courage, or perhaps the permission, to make changes and take better care of themselves.”

She describes what this looks like in practice: a shed built in the garden to unwind, a new job that actually fits, explaining to friends that a one-on-one visit is more manageable than a group gathering. “Often, when you unapologetically take care of yourself, people accept it without any issue.”

For Bianca, the experience was almost the opposite. Understanding herself was what made growth possible.

Back to physics. “Fighting yourself can never lead to real progress.” The result is exhaustion. “I’m happy if I can live my life without constant alarm bells going off in my mind, or without constant self-monitoring. That, to me, is peace.”

item.title: The Trouble With Time-Outs
item.description:
Parenting

The Trouble With Time-Outs

What to try instead of time-outs.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Misbehavior is an expression of an overwhelmed brain.
  • Effective discipline involves teaching children about desired behaviors. Time-outs don't do that.
  • Children need to learn what to do, not what not to do.

In theory, time-outs make sense. The goal of a time-out is to remove a child from an environment where unwanted behavior has occurred. The new environment is free of toys and attention from others. The new environment is boring. It is calm and quiet and mimics the emotional state you would like your child to emulate. The goal of a time-out is to provide a child with an opportunity to self-regulate and then return to normal life and their previous environment. In practice, however, successful time-outs are much more challenging and frustrating, particularly with young or strong-willed children.

Imagine this familiar scene: Your preschooler steals the Play-Doh your older child was playing with. Your child knows that stealing toys from other children is a no-no. You announce, “Time-out!” and point toward the designated chair.

Your child refuses to go.

Eventually, you carry them to the time-out chair. They immediately get up and run away. You chase after them and physically put them in the chair. They run away again. Before long, your child's original behavior is forgotten because the two of you are locked in a power struggle over sitting in a chair.

Why Time-Outs Can Go Wrong

One of the biggest problems with time-outs is the parental expectation that children will be compliant with them.

Parents may picture a child sitting quietly and thinking: I shouldn't have taken that toy. Next time I'll ask my mom for help.

That is a completely unrealistic expectation. A young child does not possess the executive functioning skills that are sophisticated enough for those types of thoughts. In fact, a young child may view being put in a time-out as a threat to their very existence. Their behavior may worsen instead of improve.

Skills such as emotional regulation, impulse control, empathy, and problem-solving develop gradually. A dysregulated toddler or preschooler generally doesn't have the ability to independently analyze their misbehavior, identify how they should have acted instead, and formulate a better plan for next time.

There is another potential problem. When time-outs involve yelling, threats, or rejection (whether physical or emotional), the experience can shift from discipline toward punishment. A child may stop hearing, My behavior wasn't acceptable and instead start to believe, Something is wrong with me.

Those are very different messages.

Regulation Needs to Happen Before Learning Can Occur

Childhood misbehavior is an expression of an overwhelmed brain. It is not a sign of defiance, and it is certainly not malicious. The nervous system needs an opportunity to calm down before real change can occur.

Think about adults. If you are angry, tired, hungry, or overstimulated, you probably will not be very receptive to a discussion with your partner who tells you that you loaded the dishwasher incorrectly. Children are no different—and they have far less ability to regulate their emotions or behaviors.

The Heart of the Matter

The underlying problem with traditional time-outs is that they do not teach children how to behave more appropriately in the future. Successful time-outs remove a child from a stimulating situation after a problematic behavior occurs, provide the opportunity for self-regulation, and then the child returns to their original environment.

A child’s brain may not be developed enough to associate misbehavior with the need for emotional regulation and redirection. Furthermore, what has a child learned from being put in a time-out? Probably nothing. If no one tells them what the desired future behavior is, how are they going to learn?

The biggest problem with time-outs? They don’t teach children the behaviors we actually want them to learn.

Try This Approach Instead

If your child misbehaves, let them self-regulate. They may have a temper tantrum. That’s okay. After everyone is calm, reconnect with your child and briefly revisit what happened. You might say: “It seems like you were angry when your brother took your toy. It's okay to feel angry. It's not okay to hit, push, or steal that toy back. Hitting hurts. Next time, come get me for help.”

Notice how much information that brief conversation provides. The child learns the name of their emotion, the behavioral boundary, the consequences of their action, and—perhaps most importantly—what they can do differently next time. Will this approach work the first time you do it? Probably not. But repeated consistently, over time, it will make all the difference. Effective discipline becomes an opportunity to teach rather than simply a consequence to endure.

Look for What Happened Before the Behavior

People don't behave in a vacuum. Universal triggers for misbehavior include being hungry, tired, being angry, and being overstimulated. Your child may have additional triggers for misbehavior. Try to identify and avoid them.

Recognizing triggers isn't “giving in.” It is understanding the capabilities of the child standing in front of you and working with the child that you have. Pack snacks. Do your best to ensure children are getting enough sleep. Bring toys and activities for long waits. Prepare children for transitions well in advance. Prevention is an underrated form of discipline.

What If Time-Outs Work for Your Child?

None of this means every family must abandon time-outs. They do work for certain children. Some children respond well to a brief break from an overstimulating environment. If you choose to use time-outs, keep them calm, consistent, and limited to three to five clearly defined behaviors that are unwanted. Avoid yelling, shaming, or turning the process into a power struggle.

Discipline has a larger goal. As parents, we are not simply trying to stop unwanted behavior in the moment. We're trying to raise children who develop emotional intelligence, understand the consequences of their actions, and learn how to behave in a kinder, more compassionate manner in the future.

item.title: How to Live With an Anxious Partner
item.description:
Anxiety

How to Live With an Anxious Partner

Cope with a partner’s anxiety without missing out on important life experiences.

Posted August 28, 2026

Key points
  • Anxious individuals often avoid activities that make them uncomfortable.
  • Spouses and partners may experience a constricted lifestyle if they accommodate this avoidance of activities.
  • Resentment associated with missing out on important life experiences may threaten the relationship.
  • Encouraging loved ones to overcome their fears rather than avoiding them will improve their mental health.

Individuals who consistently experience excessive anxiety in daily life often cope by avoiding activities and places that increase their feelings of anxiety. The partners and spouses of these individuals often experience increased anxiety as a result of their empathy towards their loved one and enable the constriction of their lifestyle as more and more activities and places are avoided. The long-term effect of this strategy is two very anxious individuals living in a very small world, missing out on much that life has to offer. This can threaten the integrity of the relationship as resentment builds as the previously non-anxious partner sacrifices more and more to quell their loved one’s anxiety. Learning how to address your partner’s anxiety without giving in to it will support the integrity of the relationship while minimizing the avoidance of life activities.

Chronic excessive anxiety can be the result of many different causes. A history of trauma, neurochemical imbalance, and lack of self-confidence are very frequent drivers. Responding to your loved one’s anxiety by cooperating with their attempt to avoid stressful situations gives short-term relief but makes the situation worse in the long term. Cooperation with the avoidance reinforces the legitimacy of the fear or anxiety and the avoidant solution to it. This tends to result in increased sources of anxiety and increased avoidance. The healthy solution is to compel your loved one to address the anxiety at its source rather than yield to it by giving in to avoidance.

Source: Mooremeditation / Pixabay

For example, Ellen met Rich at a county fair. She lived in a big city but had gone to the fair every year since she was a little girl. Rich worked at the fair, and they hit it off immediately. The fair lasted three days, and Ellen met Rich every night after the fair closed, and they enjoyed each other’s company at local bars and restaurants.

When the fair closed for the year, Ellen invited Rich to go out with her in the city. He expressed that he would love to see her but was not comfortable in crowded areas. She got weary of having to drive out of the city to see him. He finally agreed to see her in the city but only if he went directly to her apartment and they ordered takeout delivery so he didn’t have to cope with crowds. At first, Ellen thought this was a reasonable compromise, and they spent many evenings in her apartment.

Ellen was a very social person and had many friends. She got invitations to parties, weddings, and other events, but Rich refused to go because the crowds made him nervous. Ellen declined numerous invitations because she didn’t want to go without Rich, and eventually, her friends stopped inviting her.

Rich asked Ellen to move in with him. She wanted to live with him, but he was unwilling to live in the city, or even in an apartment, because there were too many people. She found herself living with him in a rural area with few neighbors. He became more uncomfortable with crowds and refused to go to bars, restaurants, or even supermarkets. They barely ever left the house. Ellen loved Rich, but the isolation became unbearable. She eventually left him, even though she loved him, to go back to the city and reunite with her friends.

Empathizing Without Absorbing Anxiety

The first step is to learn how to empathize with your partner without absorbing their anxiety. You are compassionate about their suffering but not accepting of the associated limitations. You encourage them to seek help so that they can join you in your activities rather than giving up your activities to placate them. Stop validating avoidance as a reasonable way to cope with discomfort.

Encourage Your Loved One to Conquer Their Fears

Ellen should have encouraged Rich to get help for his anxiety while going to her friend’s events without him, until he could join her. She should validate Rich’s anxiety but insist that he get well, rather than her getting sick and becoming avoidant like him and with him. She should offer to support his efforts to combat his anxiety by facilitating good treatment and supporting him while he pursues it.

Be prepared for some pushback, particularly if you have been giving in to the avoidance for a significant period of time up until now. Here is a typical dialogue and how you might respond. L1 refers to your loved one.

L1: If you really cared about me, you wouldn’t try to get me to do things that make my anxiety worse.

You: It is because I do care about you that I am encouraging you to overcome your fears rather than giving in to them.

L1: I can’t. I will panic and fall apart.

You: I will be there with you. You will not be alone. I know this is hard, but I know that you can do it, and must do it.

L1: Obviously your party is more important to you than I am, so just go.

You: It would be easier for me to stay home and comfort you, but it is because I love you that I must push you towards health, rather than placate your anxiety.

This is very hard to do, and it probably won’t work the first time you try. You must be consistent and stalwart while also being compassionate and understanding. If you are consistent, you give your loved one and your relationship the best chance of duration and fulfillment. If your loved one chooses to be ill rather than be with you, then they are not ready to heal and grow.

You will have to decide how long it is healthy for you to continue encouraging them to heal and when you need to move on. If you sacrifice your own growth for someone else’s choice to cling to illness, you will both lose.
